mcqs.q: Development of the periodontal ligament begins:
opts: With root formation, prior to tooth eruption
Only after the tooth reaches occlusion
mcqs.explain: The PDL begins to develop with root formation, before the tooth erupts, as HERS grows apically between the dental papilla and follicle.

mcqs.q: The cells that give rise to the periodontal ligament come from the:
opts: Dental follicle (between alveolar bone and HERS)
mcqs.explain: Dental follicle cells located between the alveolar bone and Hertwig's root sheath form the PDL; they include the dental follicle proper and perifollicular mesenchyme.

mcqs.q: The undifferentiated stem cells retained in the PDL can differentiate into:
mcqs.explain: PDL stem cells retain the potential to differentiate into osteoblasts, cementoblasts and fibroblasts — the cells that build the periodontium.

mcqs.q: Which principal fibre group is the FIRST to develop?
mcqs.explain: The first collagen bundles to become discernible are the precursors of the alveolar crest fibre group; the apical group then establishes the definitive architecture.

mcqs.q: The definitive PDL architecture is established with the formation of the:
mcqs.explain: With formation of the apical fibre group, the definitive periodontal ligament architecture is established.

mcqs.q: At the time of first occlusal contact, the oblique fibres are:
opts: Still being formed in the middle third (mature progressively from the apex thereafter)
mcqs.explain: At first occlusal contact the horizontal group is nearly complete, while the oblique fibres in the middle third are still forming; they mature progressively from the apex as occlusion is established.

mcqs.q: How many broad functional categories does the PDL serve?
opts: Six (physical, supportive, homeostatic, sensory, eruptive, nutritive)
mcqs.explain: The PDL has six functions: physical, supportive, homeostatic (formative/remodelling), sensory, eruptive and nutritive.

mcqs.q: Which is a PHYSICAL function of the PDL?
mcqs.explain: Physical functions include a protective soft-tissue casing, transmission of occlusal force, attachment, maintenance of gingival relations and shock absorption.

mcqs.q: The arrangement of the principal fibres resembles a:
mcqs.explain: The principal fibres are arranged like a suspension bridge or hammock, suspending the tooth in its socket.

mcqs.q: When an axial (vertical) force is applied to a tooth, the major part is borne by the:
opts: Oblique fibres (which straighten from their wavy pattern)
mcqs.explain: On axial loading, the oblique fibres alter their wavy, untensed pattern, assume full length, and sustain the major part of the force.

mcqs.q: In areas of TENSION during tooth movement, the principal fibre bundles are:
mcqs.explain: In tension areas the fibres become taut rather than wavy; in pressure areas the fibres are compressed and the bone distorts in the direction of root movement.

mcqs.q: The tensional theory of tooth support holds that the major supporting element is the:
opts: Principal fibres (which transmit force to the bone)
mcqs.explain: The tensional theory states the principal fibres are the major factor: they unfold, transmit force to bone causing elastic deformation, then to basal bone.

mcqs.q: According to the viscoelastic system theory, tooth displacement is largely controlled by:
opts: Fluid movements (extracellular fluid passing through the cribriform plate)
mcqs.explain: The viscoelastic theory states displacement is mainly controlled by fluid movement — extracellular fluid passes into bone marrow via foramina in the cribriform plate — with fibres playing a secondary role.

mcqs.q: The formative/remodelling function means PDL cells:
opts: Form and resorb cementum and bone, with constant turnover
mcqs.explain: PDL cells form and resorb cementum and bone during physiologic tooth movement and repair; the ligament is constantly remodelled with fibroblast and endothelial mitosis.

mcqs.q: The sensory nerve fibres of the PDL transmit their sensations via the:
mcqs.explain: The PDL is richly supplied with sensory fibres carrying tactile, pressure and pain sensations via the trigeminal pathways.

mcqs.q: Compared with other ligaments and tendons, the PDL is:
mcqs.explain: The PDL is a highly vascularized tissue relative to other ligaments/tendons, supplying nutrients to cementum, bone and gingiva and providing lymphatic drainage.

mcqs.q: A notable homeostatic feature of the PDL is its ability to:
opts: Maintain a constant width throughout life despite changing forces
Continuously increase its width with age
mcqs.explain: The PDL adapts to rapidly changing forces yet maintains a constant width — a key measure of periodontal homeostasis regulating bone, cementum and fibre formation.

mcqs.q: Which is an age change in the PDL?
opts: Decreased fibroblasts and increased elastic fibre, with reduced repair potential
mcqs.explain: Aging brings fewer fibroblasts, less organic matrix, fewer epithelial rests, more elastic fibre and decreased cell proliferation — impairing repair.

mcqs.q: When a horizontal (tipping) force is applied, the tooth rotates about an axis such that:
opts: The apical root portion moves opposite to the coronal portion
The whole root moves bodily in one direction without rotation
mcqs.explain: On a tipping force the tooth rotates about an axis; the apical portion of the root moves in the direction opposite to the coronal portion.

mcqs.q: Hertwig's epithelial root sheath, in PDL development, separates the:
opts: Dental papilla (internally) from the dental follicle (externally)
mcqs.explain: HERS forms a circumferential sheath encompassing the dental papilla and separating it externally from the dental follicle cells.

saqs.q: Outline the development of the PDL.
saqs.a: Begins with root formation before eruption; HERS grows apically between papilla and follicle; dental follicle cells form the PDL and retain stem cells (→ osteoblasts, cementoblasts, fibroblasts).

saqs.q: Describe the sequence of principal-fibre development.
saqs.a: Alveolar crest group first, then the apical group (definitive architecture); at occlusion the horizontal group is nearly complete and the oblique fibres mature from the apex.

saqs.q: List the six functions of the PDL.
saqs.a: Physical, supportive, homeostatic (formative/remodelling), sensory, eruptive and nutritive.

saqs.q: How does the PDL transmit occlusal forces?
saqs.a: Fibres act like a suspension bridge/hammock; on axial load the oblique fibres straighten and bear the force, transmitting it as tension to the bone (tension zones taut, pressure zones compressed).

saqs.q: Contrast the tensional and viscoelastic theories of shock absorption.
saqs.a: Tensional: the principal fibres transmit force to bone. Viscoelastic: displacement is controlled mainly by fluid movement (through the cribriform plate), fibres secondary.

saqs.q: Describe the nutritional and sensory functions of the PDL.
saqs.a: Supplies nutrients to cementum, bone and gingiva via its rich vasculature (+ lymphatic drainage); sensory fibres carry tactile, pressure and pain sensations via the trigeminal nerve.

saqs.q: List the age changes of the PDL.
saqs.a: Decreased fibroblasts, decreased organic matrix, decreased epithelial rests, increased elastic fibre, and decreased proliferation (impaired repair).
